lesson.title: The Converse That Fails: Continuity Without a Derivative
lesson.summary: Being continuous at a point places no guarantee on differentiability there; a function can be perfectly unbroken and still have no well-defined tangent line, as corners and cusps demonstrate.
lesson.body:
The previous section established that differentiability always implies continuity. It is tempting to assume the reverse must also hold, that any function without jumps or holes must have a derivative everywhere, but this converse statement is false, and recognizing why is essential to understanding what differentiability really requires. Continuity only guarantees that a function's value does not jump; it says nothing at all about whether the function's rate of change settles down to a single number as you approach a point.

The simplest counterexample is f(x) = |x| at a = 0. Continuity is immediate: as x approaches 0 from either side, |x| approaches 0, which equals f(0), so there is no jump, hole, or break in the graph at all. Yet as shown when one-sided derivatives were first introduced, the left-hand derivative there is -1 and the right-hand derivative is 1. Since these disagree, the two-sided derivative does not exist at 0. The graph is unbroken, you could trace it without lifting a pencil, but it has a sharp corner at the origin, and a corner has no single tangent line, hence no derivative.

This is exactly the phenomenon organized under non-differentiable points: a function can be continuous at a point while still failing to be differentiable there through a corner, a cusp, or a vertical tangent. The cusp example, f(x) equal to the square root of the absolute value of x, is continuous at 0 in the same simple way that |x| is, since the square root of a quantity approaching 0 also approaches 0, yet its one-sided derivatives diverge to opposite infinities rather than merely disagreeing as finite numbers. Continuity survives in every one of these cases; differentiability does not.

The gap between the two properties can be pushed to an extreme. In 1872, the mathematician Karl Weierstrass presented a function that is continuous at every single real number but differentiable at none of them, constructed as an infinite sum of increasingly rapid, increasingly small cosine oscillations layered on top of each other. At the time, this shocked mathematicians who had assumed that a continuous curve should at worst fail to be smooth at a handful of isolated points, the way |x| fails at just one point. The Weierstrass function showed that a graph could be unbroken everywhere and still be a corner, effectively, at every single point, with no tangent line anywhere.

The practical lesson is that continuity should never be treated as evidence of differentiability. Whenever a function is built from absolute values, roots of expressions that can equal zero, or piecewise definitions taped together, continuity has to be checked separately from differentiability, and differentiability requires its own dedicated check, comparing one-sided derivatives directly, exactly as outlined for corners, cusps, and vertical tangent points.
